content: The script needed to be adaptable to accommodate gendered language and linguistic inflections that convey respect for elders. In Guatemala, a different visual representation of the four-point response scale was required. Instead of traditional methods, interviewers used grains or dried beans and four buckets to represent the response options: one empty, one with a small amount of grain, one with a moderate amount, and one very full. Before conducting the interview, time was spent explaining these quantities to ensure participants understood the scale options. This approach ensured the survey process yielded complete, high-quality data. Survey tools and processes were refined through various methods, including door-to-door and online surveys. Written materials were adapted for individuals with disabilities or disadvantages to ensure basic accessibility. This included using plain language, large fonts, clearly readable questions and response options, as well as images and audio for visually impaired individuals. Human-centered design was employed to tailor immunization programs. Countries could add specific questions to the BeSD tools to address context-specific issues. For example, questions could explore decision-making autonomy within households, such as asking, In your household, who made the decision about vaccinating your child? Surveys were also adapted for verbal administration (read aloud by an interviewer) or self-administration (completed by the respondent). When adapting surveys for online data collection, interviewer instructions were removed, and simple instructions were included to guide respondents. Question wording and response options were kept consistent to maintain data integrity. The BeSD surveys were designed to be read aloud to respondents but could be adapted for self-completion, either on paper or online. For online adaptations, changes to question wording were evaluated to ensure understanding and to assess how changes might affect responses. The qualitative interview guides mirrored the four BeSD domains but allowed for deeper exploration of specific topics when necessary. The BeSD process (Plan, Investigate, Act) aligned with the Gavi Alliance IRMMA Framework (Identify, Reach, Measure, Monitor, Advocate) to reduce zero-dose children—those who have not received any routine vaccines. Missed communities often face barriers such as poor access to healthcare, limited economic and educational opportunities, and lack of political representation. Identifying zero-dose children required analyzing multiple data sources, including behavioral and social drivers of under-vaccination. Data collection methods were carefully chosen to ensure quality. A research protocol was developed to outline the research question, target population, sampling methods, data collection procedures, and data analysis plans. Data security was prioritized, with completed questionnaires stored securely in locked cabinets or password-protected devices. Different data collection modes had specific strengths and limitations. Face-to-face interviews allowed for longer interactions and clarification of complex questions but required significant resources and could lead to socially desirable responses. Online methods were cost-effective and reduced social desirability bias but were limited to populations with internet access and often had lower response rates. Sampling approaches, whether probability-based or non-probability-based, were selected based on study goals, resources, and the need for representativeness or rich qualitative insights. Probability sampling provided data representative of the target population but was more time-consuming and costly. Non-probability sampling was used when probability sampling was impractical or when specific insights were needed, though it limited generalizability. Sampling plans included strategies to minimize bias and ensure diverse representation, such as varying recruitment times and locations. The BeSD tools were integrated into existing population-based surveys where possible, and sampling experts were consulted to develop robust sampling plans. For qualitative studies, purposeful sampling was employed to recruit individuals with valuable experiences or characteristics relevant to the study objectives.
